title: Node Module Resolution: The Complete Handbook
summary: How Node.js turns a string in require() or import into a file on disk — the CommonJS resolution algorithm, ESM specifier rules, package.json type/exports/imports fields, dual packages, and the node_modules lookup chain. Covers mechanics, interop, trade-offs, and the mistakes that break published packages.

chapters.title: Two Module Systems, One Runtime
points: Definition: module resolution = mapping a specifier string ('fs', './util.js', 'lodash/merge') to an absolute file path or built-in module.
Node ships two loaders: CommonJS (CJS, `require`/`module.exports`, 2009) and ECMAScript Modules (ESM, `import`/`export`, standardized ES2015, stable in Node 12+).
CJS is synchronous: `require()` blocks, returns the value immediately, can appear anywhere in a function body.
ESM is asynchronous and has three phases: construction (parse + resolve all specifiers), instantiation (link live bindings), evaluation (run module bodies).
Consequence: ESM imports are hoisted and statically analyzable; `import` cannot take a runtime-computed specifier — use dynamic `import()` which returns a Promise.
CJS exports a value snapshot (`module.exports` object); ESM exports live bindings — reassigning `let count` inside a module updates every importer.
ESM specifiers are URLs under the hood: resolution produces a `file:` URL, so `%20` decoding and `?query#hash` suffixes are meaningful ('./a.js?v=2' is a distinct module instance).
Node built-ins resolve first and never hit the filesystem: 'fs', 'path', 'node:fs'. The `node:` prefix is unambiguous and cannot be shadowed by a node_modules package.
Mental model: CJS resolution = filesystem probing with extension guessing; ESM resolution = strict URL resolution with no guessing (plus package.json fields as the escape hatch).
Everything else in this handbook is the detail of those two algorithms and the package.json fields that steer them.

chapters.title: The CommonJS require() Algorithm
points: `require(X)` from module at path Y follows the spec pseudo-algorithm `require(X) from module at path Y` in the Node docs — memorize its five branches.
Branch 1: if X is a core module (or `node:`-prefixed), return the built-in and stop.
Branch 2: if X begins with './', '../' or '/', resolve against dirname(Y), then try LOAD_AS_FILE(path) then LOAD_AS_DIRECTORY(path).
Branch 3: if X begins with '#', apply the package `imports` field of the nearest parent package.json.
Branch 4: otherwise X is a bare specifier — walk the node_modules chain (next chapter).
LOAD_AS_FILE(X): try X exactly, then X.js, then X.json, then X.node (compiled addon), in that order — first hit wins.
LOAD_AS_DIRECTORY(X): read X/package.json; if it has `main`, resolve that as a file (with extension guessing), else fall back to X/index.js, X/index.json, X/index.node.
Extension guessing is why `require('./util')` works — a convenience CJS has and ESM deliberately dropped.
Order matters: a file `./util.js` beats a directory `./util/index.js`, because LOAD_AS_FILE runs before LOAD_AS_DIRECTORY.
`require.resolve(X)` runs the whole algorithm and returns the path without loading — the primary debugging tool.
`require.resolve(X, { paths: [...] })` overrides the search roots, useful for resolving as if from another directory.
Since Node 22 (`--experimental-require-module`) and by default in Node 23+, `require()` may load a synchronous-graph ESM module and return its namespace object.

chapters.title: node_modules Lookup: The Directory Walk
points: For a bare specifier, Node builds NODE_MODULES_PATHS(Y): every ancestor directory of Y with '/node_modules' appended, from deepest to the filesystem root.
Example from /app/src/a.js: /app/src/node_modules, /app/node_modules, /node_modules — tried in that order.
Directories already named 'node_modules' are skipped when building the list, so no /app/node_modules/node_modules entry.
First match wins: a nested copy shadows a hoisted one. This is how npm supports two versions of the same package in one tree.
Bare specifier splitting: 'lodash/merge' = package name 'lodash' + subpath './merge'; scoped names take two segments — '@scope/pkg/sub'.
Deep imports into a package (`require('lodash/fp/get')`) work by plain file resolution inside the package dir — unless `exports` blocks them.
Global paths (GLOBAL_FOLDERS): $HOME/.node_modules, $HOME/.node_libraries, $PREFIX/lib/node — legacy, searched last, effectively deprecated.
NODE_PATH env var prepends extra search directories; legacy, non-portable, avoid it in favor of workspaces or `imports`.

Symlinks: by default Node resolves the realpath of a linked package (`npm link`, pnpm store), so the linked package's own node_modules chain applies — `--preserve-symlinks` disables this and is a classic source of duplicate-instance bugs.
Complexity: worst case O(depth × candidates-per-dir) stat() calls per unresolved specifier; results are cached, so cost is paid once per unique specifier+parent pair.
Practical consequence: deep directory nesting plus many bare imports means many failed stat() calls at cold start — a real contributor to serverless cold-start time.
pnpm's symlinked store and npm's flat hoisting are two different strategies over the same algorithm; hoisting causes 'phantom dependencies' — code that imports a package it never declared.

chapters.title: Inside CJS: Wrapper, Cache, Circular Deps
points: Every CJS file is wrapped: `(function (exports, require, module, __filename, __dirname) { ... })` — that is why those five identifiers exist without being imported.
`module.exports` is the real export value; `exports` is only an alias parameter. `exports = {...}` rebinds the local and exports nothing — must write `module.exports = {...}`.
`require.cache` is keyed by resolved absolute filename; a second `require` of the same path returns the same object without re-executing.
Deleting `delete require.cache[require.resolve('./x')]` forces a reload — useful in tests, dangerous in production (stale references to the old object persist).
Module identity is per resolved path: the same package resolved at two paths (hoisted + nested) yields two independent instances — breaks singletons, `instanceof`, and React hooks.
Circular requires do not throw: the partially-filled `module.exports` of the in-progress module is returned, so late-defined properties are `undefined` at that moment.
Workaround pattern: require lazily inside the function that needs it, or export a function rather than destructured values.
Destructuring at require time (`const { a } = require('./circular')`) captures the snapshot and is the usual way circular bugs become permanently broken.
Wrapper example: `console.log(module.parent, require.main === module)` — the classic 'am I the entry point' check.

ESM handles cycles differently: bindings are hoisted and linked before evaluation, so a function declaration in a cycle works, but reading a `const` before its module evaluated throws a TDZ ReferenceError.

chapters.title: ESM Import Specifiers
points: Three specifier kinds: relative ('./x.js', '../y.js'), absolute-URL ('file:///abs/x.js', 'data:', 'node:'), and bare ('lodash', '@scope/pkg/sub').
Relative and absolute specifiers get NO extension guessing and NO directory-index fallback — './util' and './dir' both throw ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND. Write './util.js' and './dir/index.js'.
Rationale for strictness: browser parity, cheaper resolution (no probing), and unambiguous caching keys.
Bare specifiers use the same node_modules walk as CJS, but the package's entry comes from `exports` first, then `main`, then legacy index fallbacks.
`import.meta.url` replaces `__filename`; derive the rest: `fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)` and `path.dirname(...)`, or `import.meta.dirname`/`import.meta.filename` in Node 20.11+.
`import.meta.resolve(spec)` performs ESM resolution and returns a URL string — the ESM answer to `require.resolve`.
Dynamic `import(spec)` accepts runtime strings, returns a Promise of the namespace object, and is the only way to load ESM from CJS on older Node.
Import attributes: `import data from './x.json' with { type: 'json' }` — JSON modules require the attribute; without it Node throws ERR_IMPORT_ATTRIBUTE_MISSING.
Query strings bust the ESM cache: `await import('./mod.js?t=' + Date.now())` reloads the module (and leaks the old one — no cache eviction API).
Only `file:`, `data:`, and `node:` URLs are supported by default; `https:` imports remain experimental behind a flag.
Percent-encoding: '#' and '?' in real filenames must be encoded, since they are parsed as URL fragment/query.

chapters.title: package.json "type" and File Extensions
points: `"type": "commonjs"` (the default when absent) makes .js files parse as CJS; `"type": "module"` makes .js files parse as ESM.
Always-explicit extensions: `.mjs` is ESM regardless of `type`; `.cjs` is CJS regardless of `type`. Same for `.mts`/`.cts` in TypeScript.
The `type` field is read from the NEAREST parent package.json, walking up from the file — not from the project root or the entry point.
Consequence: dropping a `{"type":"commonjs"}` package.json into a subdirectory flips just that subtree — the standard trick for a CJS build folder inside an ESM package.
Nothing outside a package boundary matters: a file's format is decided by extension + nearest package.json, never by how it was imported.
Under `"type": "module"`: no `require`, no `__dirname`, no `module.exports`, top-level `this` is `undefined` (not `module.exports`), and top-level `await` is allowed.
Under CJS: no `import`/`export` syntax; attempting it gives 'Cannot use import statement outside a module' — the single most-seen Node module error.
Error signature the other way: ERR_REQUIRE_ESM ('require() of ES Module ... not supported') on Node versions before require(esm) landed.
Symmetric rule table row: file `a.js` + no type field = CJS; `a.js` + type module = ESM; `a.mjs` = ESM always; `a.cjs` = CJS always.
Adding `"type": "module"` to an existing package is a BREAKING change for consumers and for your own untouched .js files — bump major.
Extensionless files and files with unknown extensions are unsupported in ESM (ERR_UNKNOWN_FILE_EXTENSION) unless a custom loader handles them.

chapters.title: package.json "exports": Entry Points and Encapsulation
points: `exports` replaces `main` as the modern entry-point declaration and is honored by both the ESM and CJS resolvers (Node 12.7+ / 12.16+).
Hard encapsulation: once `exports` is present, ONLY the listed subpaths are importable. `require('pkg/lib/internal.js')' throws ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED even though the file exists.
Sugar form — a bare string is the '.' entry: `"exports": "./index.js"`.
Map form: `"exports": { ".": "./index.js", "./utils": "./src/utils.js", "./package.json": "./package.json" }`.
Always export `./package.json` — many tools read it, and encapsulation blocks them otherwise.
All target paths must be relative and begin with './'. Bare targets and absolute paths are invalid (ERR_INVALID_PACKAGE_TARGET).
Subpath patterns use a single `*` as a non-greedy wildcard on both sides: `"./features/*": "./src/features/*.js"` maps 'pkg/features/x' to src/features/x.js.
`null` targets block a subpath — useful to punch holes in a pattern: `"./features/internal/*": null`.
Key order matters: the first matching key wins for conditions; for patterns, the most specific (longest literal prefix) pattern wins.
`main` still applies for older Node and bundlers; keep it as a fallback alongside `exports`.
Trade-off: encapsulation prevents consumers depending on your internals (freeing you to refactor) but breaks the ecosystem habit of deep imports — plan subpaths deliberately.
Non-goal reminder: `exports` does not restrict what the package itself may load internally, only what outsiders may specify.

chapters.title: Conditional Exports
points: A condition map is an object whose keys are condition names and whose values are targets or nested maps; Node picks the first key it matches, in declaration order.
`"import"` matches when loaded via `import`/ESM resolution; `"require"` matches when loaded via `require()`.
`"node"` matches any Node environment; `"default"` always matches and MUST be last — later keys are unreachable.
Other standard conditions: `"node-addons"`, `"browser"` (community), `"development"`/`"production"` (enabled via `--conditions`), `"types"` (TypeScript, must come first).
Custom conditions are enabled with `node --conditions=my-cond` (alias `-C`), letting one package ship a special build for a runtime or test harness.
Canonical dual entry: `"exports": { ".": { "types": "./index.d.ts", "import": "./esm/index.mjs", "require": "./cjs/index.cjs", "default": "./esm/index.mjs" } }`.
Conditions nest with subpaths in either order: subpath map containing condition maps, or condition map containing subpath maps.
Arrays as targets provide fallbacks — first valid entry wins; rarely needed and poorly supported by older tools.
`"types"` must be listed before `"import"`/`"require"` because TypeScript also does first-match-wins ordering.
Deprecated pattern: `"module"` and `"jsnext:main"` are bundler-only conventions, not read by Node — do not rely on them for correctness.
Debug with `node --conditions=x -e "console.log(import.meta.resolve('pkg'))"` or `require.resolve` to confirm which branch is chosen.

chapters.title: "imports": Internal Aliases and Self-Reference
points: The `imports` field defines package-private specifiers; every key MUST start with '#', which is why '#' is reserved and never a node_modules name.
Example: `"imports": { "#db": { "node": "./src/db-pg.js", "default": "./src/db-memory.js" } }` then `import db from '#db'` inside the package.
Scope: only resolvable from inside the package that declares them — consumers cannot import '#db' from your package.
Targets may be relative files OR bare specifiers, so `"#lodash": "lodash-es"` is legal (unlike `exports`, which forbids bare targets).
Patterns work here too: `"#internal/*": "./src/internal/*.js"` — the modern replacement for '../../../src/internal/x.js' relative-path pyramids.
Conditions apply, enabling browser/node/test swaps without a bundler alias plugin.
Self-reference: if a package declares `exports`, it can import itself by name (`import { x } from 'my-pkg'`) and get its own public surface — good for testing the real entry.
Self-reference is only allowed when `exports` exists; otherwise ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED.
Comparison row: `imports` = private, '#'-prefixed, bare targets allowed; `exports` = public, './'-prefixed subpaths, relative targets only.
Practical use: dependency injection at resolution time (mock adapters under a custom condition), and killing deep relative paths without a build step.

chapters.title: Dual Packages: Shipping CJS + ESM
points: Definition: a dual package exposes both a CJS and an ESM build so `require()` and `import` both work.
The dual package hazard: `require('pkg')` and `import 'pkg'` load two separate copies with separate state — two class identities, two caches, two config singletons.
Symptom of the hazard: `instanceof` fails, module-level Maps diverge, event emitters never see each other's listeners.
Layout A (two builds): `./cjs/*.cjs` + `./esm/*.mjs`, wired with `import`/`require` conditions — simple, but full hazard exposure for stateful packages.

Layout B (ESM core + CJS wrapper): ship state only in the ESM build and let the CJS entry be a thin `module.exports = await import(...)` shim — impossible to do synchronously, so it needs top-level await or an async factory.

Layout C (CJS core + ESM wrapper): ship state in CJS; the .mjs file does `import cjs from './index.cjs'` and re-exports named bindings explicitly — one instance, no hazard, works everywhere. Recommended for stateful libraries.
Layout D (ESM-only): drop CJS entirely. Cleanest, but excludes consumers stuck on `require` — mitigated on Node 22+/23+ where `require(esm)` works for synchronous graphs.
The `type` trick: put `{"type":"commonjs"}` in ./cjs/package.json and `{"type":"module"}` in ./esm/package.json so plain .js output files get the right format without renaming.
Stateless packages (pure functions, no classes, no module-level state) are safe to ship as plain dual builds — decide by state, not by taste.

Publish checklist: `exports` map with types-first ordering, matching `main`/`types` fallbacks, `./package.json` exported, and a smoke test that both `require('pkg')` and `import('pkg')` return the same shape.
Verify with a tool like publint or `arethetypeswrong` before publishing — most dual-package bugs are caught statically.

chapters.title: Interop: CJS ↔ ESM
points: Importing CJS from ESM: the whole `module.exports` becomes the `default` export — `import pkg from 'cjs-pkg'` always works.
Named-export detection: Node runs cjs-module-lexer, a static analyzer, to guess named exports from CJS. `exports.a = 1` is detected; `exports[dynamicKey] = 1` is not.
When detection fails: `import { a } from 'cjs-pkg'` throws SyntaxError 'does not provide an export named a' — fix with `import pkg from 'cjs-pkg'; const { a } = pkg;`.
There is no live binding across the boundary: the CJS namespace is a snapshot taken at evaluation time.
Importing ESM from CJS classically requires dynamic `import()`: `const mod = await import('esm-pkg')` — always async, which infects the calling API.
Node 22 `--experimental-require-module`, on by default in Node 23+: `require()` of an ESM module works if the graph has no top-level await; otherwise ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE.

Under require(esm), the returned value is the module namespace object; a lone `default` export is also exposed via `module.exports.default` — check for the `__esModule`/default interop shim your bundler adds.
Bundler `esModuleInterop` (TypeScript/Babel) simulates default imports by adding `__esModule` markers — behaves differently from real Node interop and hides bugs until runtime.
ESM has no `require`; if you must, `import { createRequire } from 'node:module'; const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);` — the sanctioned escape hatch.
Comparison row — loading: CJS sync, ESM async. Bindings: snapshot vs live. Cycles: partial object vs TDZ error. Cache key: resolved path vs full URL including query.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Their Error Codes
points: ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND on './util' — missing extension in ESM. Fix: write the '.js'.
ERR_UNSUPPORTED_DIR_IMPORT on './routes' — no directory index in ESM. Fix: './routes/index.js'.
'Cannot use import statement outside a module' — file parsed as CJS. Fix: add `"type": "module"` or rename to .mjs.
ERR_REQUIRE_ESM — old Node requiring an ESM-only dependency. Fix: upgrade Node, use dynamic import, or pin the last CJS version.
ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED — deep import blocked by `exports`. Fix: use a declared subpath or ask the maintainer to export it.
ERR_UNSUPPORTED_ESM_URL_SCHEME — importing an 'https:' or Windows 'C:\...' path. Fix: use `pathToFileURL()` for absolute paths on Windows.
`__dirname is not defined` in ESM — use `import.meta.dirname` (Node 20.11+) or `fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)`.
'default is not a function' — CJS default-interop confusion; log the namespace object before destructuring.
Two copies of a package (duplicate React, duplicate Zod) — caused by version conflicts nesting a second install; diagnose with `npm ls pkg` and `require.resolve`.
Phantom dependency — importing a package that npm hoisted but you never listed in package.json; breaks under pnpm's strict layout. Fix: declare every import.
Case-sensitivity trap: `require('./User')` works on macOS/Windows and fails on Linux CI. Enforce with a lint rule.
Publishing without testing the built artifact — files excluded by the `files` field make `exports` targets point at nothing; run `npm pack` and import from the tarball.
Adding `exports` to an existing package silently breaks every consumer's deep imports — treat as a major version bump.

chapters.title: Debugging and Summary
points: Tool 1: `require.resolve('pkg')` (CJS) and `import.meta.resolve('pkg')` (ESM) — print the exact winning path.
Tool 2: `node --trace-module-resolution` / `NODE_DEBUG=module` to see the candidate paths Node probed and rejected.
Tool 3: `node -p "require.resolve.paths('pkg')"` prints the full node_modules search chain from the current directory.
Tool 4: `npm ls <pkg>` reveals duplicate versions; `npm explain <pkg>` shows why it's installed.
Tool 5: `publint` and `@arethetypeswrong/cli` validate a package's `exports`/`types` map against every consumption mode before publish.
Custom resolution: `module.register()` + a loader with `resolve`/`load` hooks (Node 20.6+) replaces the deprecated `--experimental-loader` API; used by ts-node, tsx, and mocking libraries.
Recap — CJS resolve order: core → relative file (exact, .js, .json, .node) → directory (main, index) → node_modules walk upward.
Recap — ESM resolve order: node: builtin → URL/relative (exact only) → package `imports` for '#' → node_modules walk with `exports` conditions.
Recap — format decision: extension first (.mjs/.cjs win), else nearest parent package.json `type`, else CommonJS.
Recap — the three package.json fields: `type` picks the parser, `exports` defines the public surface, `imports` defines private aliases.
Recap — dual-package rule of thumb: stateless → ship both freely; stateful → one core plus a thin wrapper, never two independent builds.
Closing heuristic: when a module error appears, ask in order — what format is this file, what did the specifier resolve to, and is there more than one copy?
